hook: A Vietnam veteran told his psychiatrist he would not take medication, because if the nightmares stopped he would have abandoned his friends. Working out why that made sense took Bessel van der Kolk the next forty years.

p: In 1978 van der Kolk started at a veterans clinic in Boston. His first patient came in on the fifth of July, having spent the previous night drinking alone in his car because the fireworks were unbearable. He was a successful lawyer with a marriage and children, emotionally absent from all of it, and more alive inside his memories of Vietnam than at his own dinner table.

Van der Kolk went to the hospital library to read up on it and found essentially nothing. The books on shell shock and war neurosis had been taken off the shelves after the Second World War on the assumption the subject was closed. Post traumatic stress did not exist as a diagnosis and would not until 1980.

The finding at the centre of everything he learned afterwards: trauma is not the story of something that happened long ago. It is the imprint that experience left on the mind, the brain and the body, firing in the present, in a body that has not received the news that the danger is over.

Think of the brain in layers. The amygdala is the smoke detector, fast and deliberately crude, triggering the alarm before you are conscious of anything. The medial prefrontal cortex is the watchtower, which can look at the whole scene and say that was a car backfiring, we are in a car park, nothing is wrong. Trauma is a durable change in that relationship. In a landmark scanner study, people with post traumatic stress were played recordings of their own trauma in the present tense. Limbic and visual areas lit up: they were not remembering, they were seeing it. The watchtower went quiet. And activity dropped in Broca's area, the speech production centre, the region a stroke damages to leave someone wordless.

Drawing on Stephen Porges, van der Kolk describes a nervous system with three levels rather than two. At the top is the social engagement system: mobile face, a voice with musical range, relaxed eye contact, a heart rate that varies gently with the breath. Below that, fight or flight. And below that, the oldest response, collapse and freeze, the body going limp in the jaws of a predator. Which level you occupy is decided by neuroception, a reading of faces, voices and movement that happens below awareness and faster than thought. In traumatised people it is miscalibrated, so neutral faces read as threats and an ordinary meeting becomes physically intolerable.

This also explains why shutdown gets mistaken for laziness. Stan and Ute Lawrence survived the same highway pile up. In the scanner his brain went into full emergency and hers went nearly blank. Both are trauma responses, and the second kind is routinely missed, because someone who has gone offline looks like someone coping.
sections.pull: Being able to feel safe with other people is probably the single most important aspect of mental health.

sections.h: The Study That Should Be Public Knowledge
p: Vincent Felitti ran an obesity clinic where patients lost enormous amounts of weight and then dropped out, specifically after succeeding. Interviewing them, he found very high rates of childhood sexual abuse, and realised the weight was functioning as protection. Losing it removed the shield, and the anxiety that followed was worse than the obesity.

With Robert Anda at the CDC he ran the Adverse Childhood Experiences study on more than seventeen thousand comfortable, insured, mostly employed adults. Ten categories of adversity, one point each. Two thirds reported at least one, and most of those reported several, because these things do not arrive alone.

The relationship to later health was a clean dose response curve, and it was not only psychiatric. Higher scores tracked with depression, suicide attempts, alcoholism and injected drug use, and also with heart disease, liver disease, lung disease, autoimmune conditions and cancer. Later analyses found the people at the top of the range had life expectancies roughly two decades shorter.

The first conclusion van der Kolk draws is that what look like self destructive behaviours are usually solutions. Smoking, overeating, drinking, drugs, self harm: in most cases these are effective short term regulators of an unbearable internal state. As Felitti put it, it is extremely hard to give up something that almost works.

Any approach that treats the behaviour as the problem, without addressing what the behaviour is managing, is fighting the wrong war. And any child whose damage came from years of an environment rather than a single event gets a scattering of separate labels instead of one accurate one. Van der Kolk proposed a developmental trauma diagnosis and the committee rejected it.

Trauma, he argues, is fundamentally the loss of agency: a nervous system that has concluded, below language, that nothing it does will change anything. Which is why telling such a person to take control of their life is a demand issued in a language their body no longer speaks.

sections.h: Why The Body Keeps The Score
p: Because it is stored as physical states rather than as narrative, trauma shows up in the body: higher rates of chronic pain, fibromyalgia, digestive disorders and autoimmune conditions, and stress hormone systems that do not switch off properly.

People also lose contact with their own internal signals. Van der Kolk describes alexithymia, having no words for feelings, and patients who genuinely cannot say whether they are anxious or angry or hungry. Brain regions involved in self sensing show reduced activity, which makes grim sense: if what is happening inside your body is unbearable, shutting off the channel that reports it is intelligent. It is also why people feel dead inside long after they are safe.
From which comes the central therapeutic claim: physical self awareness is the first step in releasing the tyranny of the past. You cannot process what you cannot feel.
sections.pull: You cannot become present in your life if you have vacated your body.

p: Top down means talking, understanding and connecting. Genuinely valuable and genuinely insufficient alone, because understanding why you flinch does not stop you flinching. Medication helps a substantial number of people, though van der Kolk is sharply critical of prescribing powerful psychiatric drugs to traumatised children.

The third road is bottom up: giving the body experiences that viscerally contradict helplessness. EMDR, which he was sceptical of until he trialled it, and which often lets people process an experience without narrating it. Trauma sensitive yoga, which improved severe long standing symptoms in his own study at a level comparable to medication trials, where the active ingredient is not the postures but the choice: nobody touches you without asking, and you decide when to stop.

Internal Family Systems, which sorts the mind into exiles carrying the pain, managers keeping life controlled so the exiles never surface, and firefighters who take emergency action when one breaks through. The firefighter that gets you drunk is not your enemy. It took a desperate job because it was the only one available, and the founding line is that there are no bad parts.

The most surprising chapter puts traumatised adolescents, including young people in the juvenile justice system, into serious theatre. The reasoning is precise, not sentimental. Trauma isolates and theatre is collective. Trauma makes you passive and acting requires agency. Trauma renders you speechless, and a script hands you enormous words for enormous feelings that are not yours to be ashamed of. A boy who cannot say a word about his rage can stand on a stage and be Macbeth.

James Pennebaker's experiments show that writing privately for fifteen or twenty minutes on consecutive days about something difficult, with no intention of showing anyone, produces measurable improvements in health markers and fewer doctor visits. The privacy is the point. And every culture in history has met collective suffering with rhythm and movement in groups. Western psychiatry is close to unique in deciding the treatment is a conversation between two people in chairs.

Held fairly: the evidence behind these therapies is uneven. The role of the eye movements in EMDR is disputed, the neurofeedback evidence is thinner than the enthusiasm suggests, and the ACE findings are correlations from retrospective self report. The central claim, that trauma is physiological and that body based treatment belongs alongside talking rather than after it, has held up well.

takeaways: Notice your body on purpose two or three times a day: where the tension sits, what your breathing is doing, whether your jaw is clenched. You cannot regulate a state you cannot detect.
Use the breath as a lever. Longer exhales than inhales engage the calming branch of the nervous system directly.
Do something rhythmic with other people every week: choir, dance, team sport, martial arts, drumming. Synchrony with other bodies does what insight alone cannot.
If you try a body based practice, choose one that is invitational, where nobody touches you without permission and you can stop at any moment. The choice is the active ingredient.
Try Pennebaker's exercise: fifteen minutes a day for three or four days, writing without editing about something difficult, then destroy the pages if you want to.
Ask what each of your worst habits is protecting you from, and what would happen if it stopped tomorrow. That addresses the fire rather than the firefighter.
When supporting someone, remember that your tone, face, pace and predictability are direct inputs into their nervous system, and matter more than what you say.
